unit.title: Classroom Dynamics, Learning Styles, and Digital Tools
unit.focus: Prompted Speaking: stimulus cards with mandatory linguistic constraints, timed production, and rapid tutor follow-up probes for adult learners moving from CEFR B1 to B2.

cards.title: Adapting Your Study Method
cards.context: You are preparing for a B2 exam and one topic has defeated every routine you have tried so far.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you had to change the way you studied because your usual method stopped working. Say what you did differently and how you knew the change helped.
sub_prompts: Which topic or skill made your original routine fail?
What exactly did you change about your routine?
What told you that the new approach was working?
What would you tell a student who wants to copy your method exactly?

mandatory_constraints.label: be going to for an intended plan
spaced repetition
a lexical field for learning strategies

functional_stems: In the end, I decided to...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said spaced repetition solved the problem. What would you say to a classmate who thinks flashcards are a waste of time?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A concession followed by a concrete reason, for example that the cards take ten minutes but remove the need to reread the whole chapter.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you show a teacher that the change actually worked, rather than just feeling better?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A measurable comparison such as a quiz score, a retention check after two weeks, or the number of errors made in a timed task.

rubric.fluency: Keeps talking for at least 90 seconds, repairing one stumble instead of falling silent.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Uses be going to for the original plan and keeps past and present forms apart.
rubric.lexical_range: Names at least four strategies with natural collocations such as break material into chunks or go over the vocabulary again.

cards.title: The Method That Did Not Work
cards.context: A teacher changed the way your class was run and the change did not suit you at all.
cards.stimulus: Describe a class where the teacher's method did not work for you. Explain what the method was, why it failed, and what you decided to do about it.
sub_prompts: What was the teacher asking you to do differently?
Why did that approach not work for you?
What did you do once you realised the method was not helping?
How did the rest of the class cope with the same method?

mandatory_constraints.label: had better for advice with a consequence
a lexical field for classroom management

functional_stems: The problem with that class was...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the teacher's method did not suit you. Which part of it worked and which part did you reject?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A clear division with a reason, for example that peer explanation worked but silent reading at home did not.

tutor_follow_up.q: If you were speaking to a new student in that class tonight, what would you tell them to do in week one?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Concrete advice attached to a consequence, for example sit near someone who asks questions so you hear the discussion first.

rubric.fluency: Speaks for 90 seconds with only one noticeable pause, using a filler such as well or the thing is.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Had better is used correctly for advice with a consequence, and reported speech stays in the past.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses classroom vocabulary precisely, for example set the pace, take part, sit in on, or take over the lesson.

cards.title: Speaking Without a Script
cards.context: Your teacher gives you two minutes to prepare and then calls on you without warning.
cards.stimulus: Describe a moment when you had to give a spontaneous presentation. Say what you were asked to talk about, how you felt, and how you structured your answer on the spot.
sub_prompts: What was the topic, and how much notice did you have?
How did you feel during the first ten seconds?
How did you organise your answer without any notes?
Did anyone else notice what happened that day?

mandatory_constraints.label: will for a spontaneous decision
stress on the first syllable in a three-syllable word
a lexical field for explaining an idea clearly

functional_stems: The moment I remember most is...
To be honest, my first instinct was to...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you structured it as you spoke. What was the very first sentence you said, and why did you choose it?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Any sensible opening that sets an order or a frame, plus awareness of why it was chosen.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you change if the same topic came back tomorrow with five minutes of preparation?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific change of approach rather than a general statement such as I would be less nervous.

rubric.fluency: Describes the moment in 90 seconds or more without losing the thread of the story.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Will is used for the instant decision made on the spot, with correct tense throughout the narration.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses explaining vocabulary such as break it down, start with the main point, or give an example.

cards.title: The App You Deleted
cards.context: One study app stayed on your phone for months and then quietly disappeared from it.
cards.stimulus: Describe a digital tool you stopped using. Explain what it was meant to do, why you abandoned it, and what you use instead.
sub_prompts: What was the tool, and who recommended it?
What made you stop opening it?
What do you use now, and is it better for you?
What does a good study tool need that this one lacked?

mandatory_constraints.label: present continuous for a fixed arrangement
a lexical field for digital tools
collocation: build a routine / set a target

functional_stems: What finally made me drop it was...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you replaced it with a paper planner. What do you gain from a tool that looks old-fashioned?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A benefit the student does not expect, such as fewer notifications or a clearer sense of completion.

tutor_follow_up.q: If a friend asked whether they should download the same app, what would you recommend?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A recommendation with a condition attached rather than a flat yes or no.

rubric.fluency: Covers the whole story in 60 to 120 seconds with at most one restart of a sentence.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Present continuous describes the fixed arrangement, and used to marks the abandoned habit.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses tool vocabulary precisely, for example sync, offline mode, log in, or interface.

cards.title: Learning From a Classmate
cards.context: A classmate in your course turned out to be a better teacher than any textbook.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you learned something important from a classmate. Say how the two of you worked together and what changed as a result.
sub_prompts: What was your classmate better at than you?
How did you actually practise together?
What changed in your work afterwards?
What did your classmate get out of teaching you?

mandatory_constraints.label: could for a tentative offer or past ability
a reflexive pronoun (herself / themselves)
collocation: keep track of progress

functional_stems: What I learned from her was...
If she had not offered, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You mentioned she taught herself to explain things aloud. What exactly did she do, and why does that work?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A description of the technique plus a reason, for example that explaining forces her to fill in the gaps she cannot recall.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you now offer her in return?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A reciprocal offer with a concrete action, such as editing her written work twice a week.

rubric.fluency: Sustains 90 seconds of connected speech with no long hesitation.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Reflexive pronouns are attached correctly to the subject, and could is used for the offer or the past ability.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses progress vocabulary such as track my errors, measure improvement, or review the week.

cards.title: When the Group Project Collapsed
cards.context: Your group had three weeks of work and only one functioning member.
cards.stimulus: Describe a group project that went wrong. Explain what happened, what it did to the group, and what you did about it.
sub_prompts: What went wrong, and how did you find out?
How did the rest of the group react?
What did you personally do to rescue the project?
What did the final result actually look like?

mandatory_constraints.label: must for internal urgency
a lexical field for group work and roles

functional_stems: The whole thing fell apart when...
I decided that someone had to...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you took charge. How did you avoid sounding pushy to the others?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Awareness of tone, such as asking rather than instructing, and the use of hedging language.

tutor_follow_up.q: What did the finished project miss, and how would you plan the next group task differently?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A concrete change to a process, such as setting deadlines in a shared file and checking them on fixed days.

rubric.fluency: Tells the story in sequence with clear time markers and no loss of meaning.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Must expresses the internal urgency and is not confused with have to for the external deadline.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses group work vocabulary such as take on a role, split the work, pull their weight, or pull something together.

cards.title: Finding Your Voice in Class
cards.context: For most of your course you listened carefully and said very little.
cards.stimulus: Describe a moment you started speaking up in class. Say what pushed you to speak, how the class reacted, and what you would tell quiet students.
sub_prompts: What made you decide to speak that day?
How did the teacher and the other students react?
What advice would you give to someone just like you?
What exactly did you say in that first contribution?

mandatory_constraints.label: a polite hedge to soften disagreement
a lexical field for classroom participation

functional_stems: The thing that pushed me was...
What I would tell them is that...

tutor_follow_up.q: You softened your point with a hedge. Was that politeness or genuine uncertainty about your own view?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Awareness of why the hedge was used and whether the speaker believes it was honest.

tutor_follow_up.q: Has speaking up changed how the teacher treats you since then?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A consequence with an example, such as being given harder questions or being asked to lead a discussion.

rubric.fluency: Reaches 90 seconds of self-directed speech rather than giving three short answers.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Hedged disagreement uses correct subjunctive and conditional forms without over-correcting.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses participation vocabulary such as chip in, put my hand up, or hold back in the discussion.

cards.title: Notes on Screen, Not on Paper
cards.context: You swapped your paper notebook for a laptop halfway through the term.
cards.stimulus: Describe the change you made to the way you take notes in class. Explain what improved, what got worse, and whether you would keep the change now.
sub_prompts: Why did you make the switch in the first place?
What worked better with the new method?
What did you lose, and would you go back?
What did you do on the days when the battery died?

mandatory_constraints.label: will for a prediction about the future
a lexical field for digital tools
a conditional (if + would / could)

functional_stems: If I had kept the paper notebook, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the screen helped you search for notes. What did it cost you in terms of attention?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A genuine trade-off, such as writing less and therefore processing the content less deeply.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you tell a student whose course still forbids laptops in lectures?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A practical workaround such as photographing slides or keeping a shared summary sheet.

rubric.fluency: Balances the two sides in 90 seconds without switching into a list of disconnected points.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Will is used for a prediction and the conditional is formed correctly with would or could.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses precise digital vocabulary such as search, split the screen, or annotate the slides.

cards.title: The Word Wall You Hit
cards.context: You could follow the grammar lesson and still freeze when it was your turn to speak.
cards.stimulus: Describe a topic you understood well but could not use in real conversation. Say how you found the gap, what you did about it, and whether it worked.
sub_prompts: Which topic was it, and how did you discover the gap?
What did you do differently to close it?
How did you measure whether it had worked?
Which new phrase do you now own because of that gap?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for learning strategies
retrieval practice
might for an uncertain possibility

functional_stems: The topic I could not use was...
I knew it had worked when...

tutor_follow_up.q: You mentioned retrieval practice. What is the difference between that and simply rereading your notes?
tutor_follow_up.probe: An explanation of active retrieval versus passive review in the student's own words.

tutor_follow_up.q: Which part of the gap was hardest to close, and why might that be?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific reasoning, such as the difference between oral fluency and written accuracy.

rubric.fluency: Speaks for at least 90 seconds with one repair rather than an abandoned sentence.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Might is used only for genuine uncertainty and is not used for requests.
rubric.lexical_range: Names strategies precisely, such as drilling question forms, shadowing a recording, or rehearsing key phrases.

cards.title: Rehearsing in the Kitchen
cards.context: Your only rehearsal space was a kitchen where your brother was also studying.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you practised a talk or performance at home. Explain where you practised, what you did, and how you got feedback.
sub_prompts: What were you preparing, and who was at home?
Where and how did you rehearse?
Did you get feedback, and did you take it?
Who helped you most, and how?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for practice and rehearsal
should for neutral advice
be going to for an intended plan

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you rehearsed in the kitchen. How did you work around the noise without losing your place?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A practical detail such as memorising an opening line or recording on a phone and checking it later.

tutor_follow_up.q: What advice did you get that you did not want to hear at the time?
tutor_follow_up.probe: An example of honest feedback and the student's eventual acceptance of it.

rubric.fluency: Describes the situation vividly in 60 to 120 seconds with natural linking words.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Should is used for neutral advice and be going to for the original plan, with no confusion between them.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses rehearsal vocabulary such as run through it, do a dress rehearsal, or go over the opening.

cards.title: A Feedback Session That Stung
cards.context: Your teacher returned your writing with a short comment and a mark you did not expect.
cards.stimulus: Describe a piece of feedback that upset you. Say what the comment was, why it affected you, and how you responded to it.
sub_prompts: What was the comment, and what did it tell you about your work?
Why did it land so hard on you?
What did you do after reading it?
Did that comment change anything in your next piece of work?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for assessment and grades
a third conditional (if + had + past participle)
a reflexive pronoun (myself / themselves)

functional_stems: If I could go back, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the mark felt unfair. What evidence would have changed your mind?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A reference to specific criteria, marker comments, or the difference between a personal judgement and a published rule.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you now give that same comment to someone else?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A softened, more actionable version that includes at least one concrete next step.

rubric.fluency: Speaks for 90 seconds even when describing an emotional moment, without switching to single-word answers.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: The third conditional is formed correctly and reflexive pronouns are attached to the right subject.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses assessment vocabulary such as mark criteria, drop a grade, or the feedback was marked clearly.

cards.title: Teaching Your Cousin The Alphabet
cards.context: A family member asked you to help them with English for free, in your own free time.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you taught someone else. Explain what you were asked to teach, how you prepared, and what worked in the teaching.
sub_prompts: Who were you teaching, and what did they want to be able to do?
How did you prepare the lesson?
Which part of your teaching actually worked?
What went wrong in that very first lesson?

mandatory_constraints.label: a reflexive verb (teach oneself / introduce oneself)
a lexical field for explaining an idea clearly
may for a tentative or formal offer

functional_stems: I was asked to help him...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the lesson worked when you stopped explaining and started asking. Why did that switch help?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A reason about learner involvement, with an example of a question the learner answered correctly.

tutor_follow_up.q: If this person asked you to teach them again next month, would you agree? What would you change?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A clear decision plus at least one concrete change to the plan.

rubric.fluency: Maintains a clear narrative through the description of the lesson in 90 seconds.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Reflexive verbs are used with the correct subject, and may is used for the offer.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses teaching vocabulary such as go through the basics, drill the vocabulary, or set up practice questions.

cards.title: The Night Before The Exam
cards.context: On the morning of your exam, the revision plan you had written was already useless.
cards.stimulus: Describe the night before an important exam. Say what your plan was, what went wrong with it, and what you actually did.
sub_prompts: What was your original plan for that night?
What made you abandon or change it?
What did you end up doing, and how do you feel about that now?
How much sleep did you actually get?

mandatory_constraints.label: have to for an external rule
precise time markers (by Friday, at the latest, once the upload finishes)
a lexical field for exam strategy

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the plan collapsed. What would you have planned if you had started two days earlier?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A realistic alternative plan with time allocations rather than generalities.

tutor_follow_up.q: How did you feel during the exam, and did that change how you performed?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A link between state of mind and performance, with a specific example of a question that went differently.

rubric.fluency: Covers the whole night in 60 to 120 seconds with clear sequencing markers.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Have to refers to the external requirement, and time markers are placed accurately.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses exam vocabulary such as past papers, mark the questions, or cover the whole syllabus.

cards.title: Switching From Textbook To Podcast
cards.context: You nearly gave up on a textbook and tried a completely different medium instead.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you changed how you got input in English. Say what you switched between, why, and how you decided whether the switch was worth it.
sub_prompts: What were you using, and what did you switch to?
Why did you make the change?
How did you judge whether the new medium was better?
How long did it take for the new medium to feel normal?

mandatory_constraints.label: a comparative structure (rather than, less + noun, not as + adjective as)
a lexical field for digital tools

tutor_follow_up.q: You compared the two media. Which one suits which kind of learner?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A generalisation with support, for example that podcasts suit learners who need a low-pressure daily routine.

tutor_follow_up.q: What is one thing the new medium is genuinely worse at?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A real limitation named without turning it into a disguised advantage.

rubric.fluency: Compares the two media in 90 seconds without repeating the same comparison point.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Comparative structures are varied rather than limited to one repeated pattern.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses input vocabulary such as comprehensible input, subtitle, or listen at double speed.

cards.title: Taking Over The Study Group
cards.context: You were the least experienced member of a study group that badly needed direction.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you took responsibility in a study group. Explain what the group was doing badly, what you changed, and how the others responded.
sub_prompts: What was the group doing poorly?
What change did you introduce?
How did the other members react to your lead?
What happened the first time you ran the session?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for group work and roles
had better for advice with a consequence
a reflexive pronoun (myself / themselves)

functional_stems: So I decided that we should...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you set a rota. How did you stop it feeling like you were ordering people around?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Examples of consultative language, such as asking for availability before assigning tasks.

tutor_follow_up.q: What happened to the group's results after the change?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A measurable or observable outcome with at least one concrete detail.

rubric.fluency: Explains the change and the reaction in 90 seconds with a clear cause and effect.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Had better is used for advice with a consequence and reflexive pronouns agree with their subject.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses role vocabulary such as assign a role, take minutes, or chair the session.

cards.title: The Teacher Who Answered Every Question
cards.context: One teacher's habit of answering her own questions shaped how the whole class spoke.
cards.stimulus: Describe a teacher whose way of running a class affected your participation. Say what the habit was, how you reacted, and what you would change about it.
sub_prompts: What was the teacher's characteristic habit?
How did it affect you and the rest of the class?
What would you change about the way questions are handled?
How did you learn to speak up in that class?

mandatory_constraints.label: sentence stress for contrast
a lexical field for classroom management
should for neutral advice

functional_stems: If I had been the teacher, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the habit killed participation. What exactly happened in the room after she answered?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A description of behaviour such as silence, shorter answers, or students holding back their questions.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you redesign the questioning so that students prepared?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A concrete mechanism such as think-pair-share, written questions first, or a rotating questioner.

rubric.fluency: Holds the topic for 90 seconds with a clear complaint and a clear proposal.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Should is used for neutral advice, and contrast is marked by word order and stress rather than by extra words.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses classroom management vocabulary such as take questions, set the pace, or invite contributions.

cards.title: Reading With A Dictionary Open
cards.context: You tried a reading strategy that made reading slower but changed how you understood the text.
cards.stimulus: Describe a reading strategy you used on a difficult text. Explain how you applied it, what it cost you, and whether you would repeat it.
sub_prompts: What was the strategy, and how did you carry it out?
What did it cost you in time or enjoyment?
Would you use it again on a new text?
What did you actually do with the words you looked up?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for learning strategies
present continuous for a fixed arrangement
vague quantifiers (a lot of, quite a few, a fair amount)

functional_stems: I decided to read it by...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said it slowed you down. What did you gain in return?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A benefit that compensates for the cost, such as noticing collocations you would have skimmed past.

tutor_follow_up.q: What kind of reader do you think you are now compared with two years ago?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A self-assessment backed by behaviour rather than a label.

rubric.fluency: Explains the method and the trade-off in 60 to 120 seconds without vague filler.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Present continuous describes the fixed reading routine and quantifiers are used with countable and uncountable nouns correctly.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses strategy vocabulary such as annotate, look up collocations, or read for gist first.

cards.title: Writing In English For The First Time
cards.context: You wrote a full page in English without translating every sentence in your head first.
cards.stimulus: Describe the first time you produced a piece of writing in English on your own. Say what you wrote, how you got started, and how you felt about it afterwards.
sub_prompts: What did you write, and who was it for?
How did you begin without translating in your head?
How did you feel when you reread it a week later?
How many drafts did that first piece take?

mandatory_constraints.label: a lexical field for writing and drafting
might for an uncertain possibility
a third conditional (if + had + past participle)

tutor_follow_up.q: You said you stopped translating. What technique replaced it?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A described technique such as thinking in single words, using a picture, or keeping a keyword list.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you tell a student who says they cannot write without translating?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Persuasive advice with a reason, plus one small practical first step.

rubric.fluency: Reflects on the experience in 90 seconds with a balance between the event and the feeling.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Might expresses genuine uncertainty and the third conditional is used correctly for the unreal past.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses writing vocabulary such as draft, redraft, put it into words, or run it past someone.

cards.title: The Tool Your School Retired
cards.context: The learning platform your school used was switched off with only two weeks of notice.
cards.stimulus: Describe a digital tool that was taken away from you. Explain what it did for you, what you had to replace it with, and how the change affected your work.
sub_prompts: What did the tool do that other tools could not?
What did you replace it with, and was the replacement worse?
How did the change affect your workload or your results?
How long did the old platform take to set up?

mandatory_constraints.label: have got to for an external rule
a lexical field for EdTech platforms and migration
a comparative structure (rather than, less + noun, not as + adjective as)

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the replacement was slower. What is one thing you were still able to do on it?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific retained function that shows careful comparison rather than blanket complaint.

tutor_follow_up.q: What will your school do differently the next time it changes a system?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A prediction with a reason, such as a migration window and a parallel run before the switch-off.

rubric.fluency: Describes the loss and the consequences in 90 seconds with a clear before and after.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Have got to refers to the institutional rule, and comparatives are formed correctly.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses platform vocabulary such as migrate, log in, export your data, or third-party integration.

cards.title: Learning From Someone Quieter Than You
cards.context: The most useful classmate in your course barely spoke in whole sentences.
cards.stimulus: Describe a time you learned something from someone who communicated in a different way from you. Explain what they taught you and how you adapted.
sub_prompts: How did this person communicate with the group?
What did you learn from them?
What did you change in your own way of working?
What did you stop doing because of that example?

mandatory_constraints.label: a reflexive pronoun (myself / themselves)
a lexical field for communication and feedback
could for a tentative offer or past ability

tutor_follow_up.q: You said they taught you by showing rather than telling. How did that change your own explanations?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A described behaviour change with an example of how the student now explains something.

tutor_follow_up.q: What might a teacher do to include students who communicate like that?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A practical suggestion such as written pair work, pre-submitted questions, or a shared group board.

rubric.fluency: Explains the difference in communication style across 90 seconds with concrete detail.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Reflexive pronouns are correctly attached and could is used for the past ability or the offer.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses feedback vocabulary such as walk someone through, show rather than tell, or write it down first.

cards.title: The Broken File Before Deadline
cards.context: A group presentation is in four hours and one of the three files will not open.
cards.stimulus: A classmate uploaded a broken file just before a group presentation deadline. State what happened, what must be done immediately, and what you are going to do next.
sub_prompts: What exactly is wrong with the file, and who does it affect?
What must be dealt with in the next thirty minutes?
Who needs to be told, and what are you going to say to them?
How much of the presentation is genuinely ready right now?

mandatory_constraints.label: must for internal urgency
be going to for an intended plan
a lexical field for file sharing and version control

functional_stems: The first thing I will do is...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the deadline was unmanageable. What would you have negotiated if you had started the conversation a week earlier?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific ask such as a staged deadline, a practice slot, or a shared template from the outset.

tutor_follow_up.q: How do you make sure the same thing never happens again with this group?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A process change such as a shared folder with naming rules and a version checklist.

rubric.fluency: Delivers the whole situation in 90 seconds in the order of events, urgency and plan.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Must marks the internal urgency while be going to marks the intended next step, and the two are not swapped.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses file vocabulary such as corrupted file, shared drive, file name, or restore an earlier version.

cards.title: Wi-Fi Dies During The Online Exam
cards.context: You are twenty minutes into a timed online exam when the connection drops completely.
cards.stimulus: Your internet connection fails in the middle of a timed online exam. Say what happens next, what you must do, and what you would tell the coordinator afterwards.
sub_prompts: What can you still do while you are disconnected?
What must you do in the first five minutes?
What would you write to the coordinator once you are back online?
Does the exam platform save your answers as you go?

mandatory_constraints.label: have to for an external rule
a schwa in the unstressed ending
precise time markers (by Friday, at the latest, once the upload finishes)

functional_stems: As soon as I could, I...

tutor_follow_up.probe: An explanation of how the same course design works differently at different levels.

tutor_follow_up.q: What is the most useful question a student could ask before paying for a course like this?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A single targeted question, such as about feedback turnaround time or support.

rubric.fluency: Reconciles the two reviews in 90 seconds without simply dismissing either one.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: The second conditional is used for the imagined reading, and hedging verbs are used with accurate complements.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses course vocabulary such as module, enrolment, tutor feedback, or self-paced.

cards.title: The Attendance Policy Statement
cards.context: A policy statement sets out exactly how attendance affects the final grade.
cards.stimulus: A course policy states that students who miss more than eight per cent of sessions will have their participation mark capped. React to it: state your position, the evidence you would bring, and the trade-off.
sub_prompts: What exactly does the policy require, and who does it affect most?
What evidence supports or challenges the rule?
What trade-off would you accept in order to keep attendance high?
How many sessions does the course have in total?

mandatory_constraints.label: must for internal urgency
a lexical field for assessment and grades
a conditional (if + would / could)

functional_stems: If I could change one clause, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said illness is the hardest case to handle. What would a fairer rule look like?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific alternative with a mechanism, such as evidence-based exemptions for illness.

tutor_follow_up.q: What does low attendance tell you about a course, and what does it not tell you?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A distinction between engagement and ability, with an example from the student's own record.

rubric.fluency: Argues the policy in 90 seconds with a clear judgement and one amendment.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Must expresses the internal obligation and the conditional is correctly formed for the alternative rule.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses policy vocabulary such as capped mark, attendance record, exemption, or justification.

cards.title: The Cheating Question
cards.context: A forum post asks whether using a translator during an online test counts as cheating.
cards.stimulus: A forum post asks whether using a translation tool during a timed online test counts as cheating. React to it: state your position, the evidence you would bring, and the trade-off you see.
sub_prompts: Who is the rule actually written for, and who does it affect most?
What would you say to a student who feels the rule is unfair?
What compromise, if any, would you accept?
Has anyone been caught using a tool before?

mandatory_constraints.label: a modal of deduction (might / may / could)
a lexical field for academic integrity and AI use
an indirect request

functional_stems: I would separate two things here...
If I were the teacher, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the rule is unclear. What wording would make it clear?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A draft rule that states precisely when tools are and are not allowed.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you respond to a student who admits they used a tool?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A practical next step with a proportionate consequence, delivered without shaming.

rubric.fluency: Responds to the forum post in 90 seconds with a clear position and a workable compromise.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Deduction modals show graded certainty and the indirect request is politely formed.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses integrity vocabulary such as unauthorised aid, declare the use, or open book.

cards.title: Two Definitions Of Learning Style
cards.context: Two textbooks define the same term in ways that cannot both be right.
cards.stimulus: Two textbooks define a learning style in ways that contradict each other: one says you have one fixed style, the other says styles are situational. React: give your position, your evidence, and the trade-off between them.
sub_prompts: What does each definition imply about how you should be taught?
What evidence from your own experience fits one and not the other?
What practical difference does the disagreement actually make, and which definition would you argue for?
Which definition did your own school use?

mandatory_constraints.label: a conditional (if + would / could)
a lexical field for learning strategies
a hedging lexical set (argue, claim, suggest)

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the fixed-style idea is misleading. What is a better way to describe what students actually do?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A more accurate description, for example a preference that shifts with the task and the mood.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you say to a student who has been told they are a visual learner?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Advice that protects the student's motivation while correcting the label.

rubric.fluency: Weighs the two definitions in 90 seconds and reaches a usable conclusion of your own.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Deduction modals express probability and the comparative structures are accurate.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses learning vocabulary such as preference, adapt, or match the task to the strategy.

cards.title: The Screenshot And The Notebook
cards.context: A short case describes how two students prepared for the same test.
cards.stimulus: A short case study compares two students: one kept photographs of every slide, the other wrote three pages of notes from memory after class. React to the case: give your position, your evidence, and the trade-off.
sub_prompts: What did each student's method actually train them to do?
What evidence in the case supports your reading?
Which method would you keep, and what would you add to it?
What actually happened in the exam itself?

mandatory_constraints.label: retrieval practice
a modal of deduction (might / may / could)
a past modal for speculation (must have / might have / should have)

functional_stems: In the case, the difference is...
I would read the evidence like this...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the second student recalled more. What might the case be leaving out?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A critical observation such as prior knowledge, available time, or the difficulty of the course.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you do differently from both students?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A third method that combines elements and states why you chose it.

rubric.fluency: Analyses the case in 90 seconds with a reading of the evidence and a personal plan.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Past modals for speculation point backwards and deduction modals express present probability.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses strategy vocabulary such as recall, photograph the slides, or write it up afterwards.

cards.title: A Classroom Without Laptops
cards.context: A school has decided that students may not use any digital device in the main classroom.
cards.stimulus: A school has banned all digital devices in the main classroom, arguing that students think better without them. React: state your position, the evidence you would bring, and the trade-off you accept.
sub_prompts: What does the school gain and what does it lose with this rule?
What evidence would settle the argument for good?
What would you change, and what would happen if the school piloted a limited use of devices?
How much of the learning there depends on screens?

mandatory_constraints.label: a second conditional (if + past simple + would)
a lexical field for digital tools
should for neutral advice

tutor_follow_up.q: You said the rule works for some subjects. Which ones, and why those?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A reasoned distinction based on the type of task rather than on subject naming alone.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you defend a limited use of devices to the school?
tutor_follow_up.probe: An argument with evidence and a pilot design that could be tested in one term.

rubric.fluency: Argues both sides of the policy in 90 seconds and commits to a clear position.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Should gives neutral advice and deduction modals mark what might follow from each option.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses policy vocabulary such as device-free lesson, classroom policy, or digital literacy.

cards.title: The Cost Of An Academic Year Of Tools
cards.context: A course budget has to cover licences, devices and training for one academic year.
cards.stimulus: A department must choose where to spend a limited budget: licences for a study platform, devices for students, or training for teachers. React to the trade-off: give your position, your evidence, and what you would give up.
sub_prompts: What does each option buy, and who does it benefit?
What evidence from experience would support your choice?
What would you give up, and who would be worst affected?
How many students are in the group this affects?

mandatory_constraints.label: must for internal urgency
a lexical field for budgets and resources
a comparative structure (rather than, less + noun, not as + adjective as)

functional_stems: If the budget were mine to divide, I would...
The case for training rests on...

tutor_follow_up.q: You chose devices over licences. What is the strongest argument against you?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A genuine counter-argument, such as licences without trained teachers producing very little change.

tutor_follow_up.q: What would you need to see in a pilot before committing the full budget?
tutor_follow_up.probe: Success measures and a timeframe, for example a comparison of grades before and after.

rubric.fluency: Justifies the budget decision in 90 seconds with evidence and a named trade-off.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: Must expresses the binding constraint and comparatives are accurate and varied.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses budget vocabulary such as allocate, prioritise, licence fee, or cost per student.

cards.title: Two Opinions On Silent Discussion
cards.context: Two teachers disagree about the value of silent written discussion in class.
cards.stimulus: Two teachers disagree about silent written discussion: one says it gives quiet students their voice, the other says it kills spontaneous speech. React: state your position, your evidence, and the trade-off.
sub_prompts: What does silent discussion actually change in a classroom?
What evidence from your own experience supports one view?
What would you combine from the two approaches?
How long does the silent phase usually last in your class?

mandatory_constraints.label: falling intonation for a wh-question
a lexical field for speaking turns and discussion
a second conditional (if + past simple + would)

functional_stems: I lean towards the first teacher because...
If the class did both, I would...

tutor_follow_up.q: You said quiet students benefit. What happens to them once the writing stops and speaking starts?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A specific prediction about performance under pressure and what would prevent it.

tutor_follow_up.q: How would you introduce a discussion format that supports both kinds of learner?
tutor_follow_up.probe: A staged procedure with a set time for writing and a set time for speaking.

rubric.fluency: Weighs the two opinions in 90 seconds and proposes a workable combination.
rubric.grammar_accuracy: The second conditional is correct for the imagined classroom, and wh-questions carry the right intonation.
rubric.lexical_range: Uses discussion vocabulary such as write it down first, take turns, or speak up in pairs.
